objectives: Map each phoneme to an appropriate grapheme.
Spell new /f/ CVC words from dictation.
Identify and repair vowel or final-sound spelling errors.
concepts: Encoding moves from spoken phonemes to written graphemes.
Every phoneme in a regular CVC word needs representation.
Vowel accuracy is essential for distinguishing CVC words.

definitions.definition: Representing spoken language with written symbols.
Breaking a spoken word into its individual sounds.
A letter or group of letters representing a sound.

commonMistakes: Substituting one short vowel for another.
Writing a guessed word without segmenting.
Confusing a spoken sound with a letter name.

basic: Dictate regular /f/ CVC words and segment before writing.
conceptual: Compare spellings that differ only in the middle vowel.
application: Repair misspelled /f/ CVC words by locating the incorrect phoneme-grapheme mapping.
higherOrderThinking: Explain why segmentation reduces spelling errors.
mixedReview: Mix /f/ CVC spelling with previously learned consonants.

formulaOrFactBank: CVC spelling = one grapheme mapped for each phoneme in the regular word.
mistakeBasedRevision: If the vowel is wrong, rehear and isolate the middle phoneme before rewriting.
weakTopicRevision: Practice the weakest short-vowel family with fresh dictation items.

activities.name: Sound boxes
steps: Push one counter for each phoneme.

activities.name: Dictation repair
steps: Have learner segment and write it.
Circle the incorrect mapping if any.

activities.name: Vowel contrast writing
steps: Dictate two words with different short vowels.

outcomes: Learner maps phonemes to graphemes in spelling.
Learner repairs common vowel and final-sound errors.

questions.question: Why is sound-to-letter mapping important for spelling?
options: It connects each heard phoneme to the grapheme used to represent it
It removes the need to listen

questions.question: A learner writes “fot” for /f/ /ɒ/ /g/. What is the likely repair?
options: Rehear the final /g/ and map it to the final grapheme
